pr_title: Bluetooth: Host: Add API to clean BT settings
pr_comments: Shouldn't the Bluetooth subsystem do this automatically upon init? Introducing an explicit public API creates the need for applications to figure out when to call it, not to mention that the inconsistency in storage might not be the application's fault at all. It also seems arbitrary to leave mesh  of the scope. What's the solution for inconsistent storage for mesh, or for non-Bluetooth related data for that matter?

> Shouldn't the Bluetooth subsystem do this automatically upon init? Introducing an explicit public API creates the need for applications to figure out when to call it, not to mention that the inconsistency in storage might not be the application's fault at all. It also seems arbitrary to leave mesh of the scope. What's the solution for inconsistent storage for mesh, or for non-Bluetooth related data for that matter?

The problem might be that this will take too much time - writing to flash - at an infortunate time. That's why we thought it'd be better for the app to decide when to do GC.

> It also seems arbitrary to leave mesh of the scope. What's the solution for inconsistent storage for mesh, or for non-Bluetooth related data for that matter?

I discussed it with @PavelVPV, they might do it differently with their own settings layer.

This seems to be non-trivial to implement without a way to delete settings keys while loading them and trying to respect MISRA (ie no malloc).
This issue does not seem to be an actual problem for devices in the field (for now).

We are not happy with the current solution (w/ @alwa-nordic and @jori-nordic) so will close the PR.

issue_context.title: Bluetooth: settings: Possible Bluetooth settings leftovers
comments: Similar issue related to storing Bluetooth data as multiple entries could occur for `save_id` function. There could be an edge case leading to storing only the new ID, but leaving the old IRK.

> Application needs a way to make sure that Bluetooth settings data is consistent and contains no leftovers:
> 
> 1. We could introduce an API to let application trigger the Bluetooth settings cleanup or retrieve information about all of the the leftover records (for example get all of the related settings keys).
>   Application could manually delete the leftovers.
>
> [...]
>
> I would suggest to follow the 1st proposed approach.
> If the leftovers are caused only by some edge cases that are not likely to happen, an application API to trigger settings data cleanup may be a reasonable approach I think (if an application does not use it, there would be no additional memory overhead too).

I think `CONFIG_BT_SETTINGS` has to 'just work'. So, the cleanup must be automatic. I believe it's good to have the stack be powerloss-safe by default.

> We could introduce a mechanism ensuring that set of related settings records is always modified together.
For example, we may store an additional settings record informing that the unpair operation for given bond is started and delete it as soon as operation is complete.
If the operation is interrupted by e.g. a power down, it could be properly finalized on subsequent boot (e.g. when settings are loaded).

This could be done by the settings API, ie a `settings_transaction_begin` and `_end` so we can update groups of settings at the same time. If the power is cut, then the settings backend is free to garbage-collect the incomplete data.

Please remind that the settings subsystem is not responsible for how a subsystem is using it. If the bluetooth subsystem is leaving garbage in the settings backend it is the responsability of the bluetooth subsystem to clean this up. If the written data is incomplete (some part written, other not) this is the responsability of the subsystem (there is no way for the settings subsystem to figure this out).

Introducing a `settings_transaction_begin` an `_end` is not a good idea as the settings backend can be on a "circular buffer" that would move the `settings_transaction_begin` to the front of the buffer while leaving the `_end` at the end of the buffer. If data is grouped they should be stored together.

> Please remind that the settings subsystem is not responsible for how a subsystem is using it. If the bluetooth subsystem is leaving garbage in the settings backend it is the responsability of the bluetooth subsystem to clean this up. If the written data is incomplete (some part written, other not) this is the responsability of the subsystem (there is no way for the settings subsystem to figure this out).

Agree. There has been also problem reported that after update to app that no longer uses some settings, these are left behind taking storage place. Settings does not know what is useful and what is not, and what is used by which subsystem so it is hard to have one cleanup solution that will not break something up. Subsystems should cleanup after themselves. Updated application should have mechanisms to discard keys, which have been used by previous versions, and are no longer used.

> 
> Introducing a `settings_transaction_begin` an `_end` is not a good idea as the settings backend can be on a "circular buffer" that would move the `settings_transaction_begin` to the front of the buffer while leaving the `_end` at the end of the buffer. If data is grouped they should be stored together.

Agree.

> This could be done by the settings API, ie a `settings_transaction_begin` and `_end` so we can update groups of settings at the same time. If the power is cut, then the settings backend is free to garbage-collect the incomplete data.

Maybe use settings for this, for example use `some/path/to/settings/sosb=<num>` for start of settings block, then you write all settings as `some/path/to/settings/<num>/some_keys` and complete it with `some/path/to/settings/<num>/eosb=num`

Then at read you search for `some/path/to/settings/sosb` to get `<update_num>` and then for `some/path/to/settings/<update_num>/eosb`.
If you do not get the `eosb` then you know that data block is incomplete and need to try with lower <update_num> to recover.
If you get the `eosb` then you have all data and can now discard all blocks with lower update number.

In order to do something like this one needs to know what data needs to be grouped, if this is already known it is much simpler to store them together. Introducing such a storage will increase the space needed, as most of the space is needed for the "name" and this is duplicated

I realized: we want to have a data-journaling file-system. We could have a `journal/<transaction_id>/data/some/path` that we would write to to form a transaction. Then we write `journal/transaction_id/commit`. Then we copy over data from the `journal/<transaction_id>/data/` to `/some/path`. On boot fsck, we check each `journal/<transaction_id>/commit`. If exists, we know it's a interrupted copy, and we do the copy again from the start. If it does not, we delete the transaction as failed/incomplete. Once the copy is done, we delete the transaction.

EDIT: We would also need a `journal/<transaction_id>/deletes/`.

> I realized: we want to have a data-journaling file-system. We could have a `journal/<transaction_id>/data/some/path` that we would write to to form a transaction. Then we write `journal/transaction_id/commit`. Then we copy over data from the `journal/<transaction_id>/data/` to `/some/path`. On boot fsck, we check each `journal/<transaction_id>/commit`. If exists, we know it's a interrupted copy, and we do the copy again from the start. If it does not, we delete the transaction as failed/incomplete. Once the copy is done, we delete the transaction.

Exactly why do you want (need) a data-journaling file-system ? If you really need it, probably settings is not the best solution for your problem.

I'm not fully sure we need data-journaling. I agree we should not jump for the big gun if not needed :P. It was just my idea of a simplistic[^1] way to have transactions like @jori-nordic mentioned. And, I'm not at all insisting that the settings subsystem needs to implement this. It could be our own layer / library. It's better if the settings subsystem is simple.

[^1]: It may be more complicated if we want a read lock for "transactional" reads as well.
@jori-nordic Shall we make a manifest of what the Bluetooth subsystem stores in settings currently, and look at what really needs to be atomic?

> 
> EDIT: We would also need a `journal/<transaction_id>/deletes/`.

What will this be used for?

> > EDIT: We would also need a `journal/<transaction_id>/deletes/`.
> 
> What will this be used for?

E.g. Deleting an identity.

I've been running into such issues where no more space is left (for SC data in my case):
E: unable to save SC: no cfg left

It can get quite hard to deal with and to recover from, because it basically prevents further pairing from new devices. In addition to the possible reset during bt_unpair cause, I believe that MAC randomization may also cause side effects with the BT_SETTINGS subsystem, as I tend to get these errors more often when using latest Android or iOS central devices.

> I've been running into such issues where no more space is left (for SC data in my case): E: unable to save SC: no cfg left
> 
> It can get quite hard to deal with and to recover from, because it basically prevents further pairing from new devices. In addition to the possible reset during bt_unpair cause, I believe that MAC randomization may also cause side effects with the BT_SETTINGS subsystem, as I tend to get these errors more often when using latest Android or iOS central devices.

This is a problem with software leaving keys they no longer use or know about, for various reasons.
Settings can not remove anything, because it does now know who the data belongs to, it just reads and stores.

When software moves away from some keys, the version that does that (and probably two next versions) should search for the keys they no longer use and remove them.

review_comments: Should we delete when this happens? RFC

I am not sure that we want to delete in this case. Maybe the user misconfigured its device and will update the configuration when it see the error.

Also I prefer to miss some items rather than delete good items.

Maybe we could use create the `is_supported_bt_key` function instead (`mem_eq` is quite ambiguous name)?
That would also allow us to also limit scope of `bt_settings_keys`.
Was actually thinking the same during my review
Consider adding explanation - e.g. `Bluetooth Mesh manage their settings themselves and have their own layer on top of the settings.`

This seems like something that should be placed other places as well. 

We should perhaps generally recommend (if not already) that applications do not use the `bt/` namespace for their BT settings?

Actually, I think that sharing a settings namespace between an application and any Zephyr subsystem is a bad idea (applications need to use their own namespaces). Maybe we could assume that user should not do it?

There is a bug in the DUT due to how `strncmp` is used. The following is a test case to prove it.

```suggestion
	settings_save_one("bt/i", &dummy_value, sizeof(dummy_value));
```

Actually that's a bug in `bt_settings_load_direct_cleanup`, thanks for catching it!

When testing if a key is known or not, here:
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/03e3c73ee32c0a3c536a4657dfe171163f05128e/subsys/bluetooth/host/settings.c#L337-L341

I compare the two strings with the size of the one we want to test. That's wrong, I should compare with the size of the string in `bt_settings_keys`. Because here it compare with `bt/id` but with the size of `bt/i`, so it say that the key is known.

I'll fix that and add the test.

Now it's wrong the other way. Comparing strings in C is hard :P

```C
settings_save_one("bt/idd", &dummy_value, sizeof(dummy_value));
```
Indeed, it should be better now. If `strncmp` say that the string are equal I then check the expected last character of the tested key to see if it's `\0` or `/`.
I am not sure of the use case. Maybe we could simply add `LOG_WRN` for each deleted setting?

> I am not sure of the use case. 

If I am a user and I have my settings stored in flash, I'd perhaps rather be aware of an issue in my settings before deleting them, rather than just silently deleting them, e.g. if I store my own settings and that I am foolish enough to store something under `bt/id` myself, then I'd rather become aware of that, rather than it just silently getting deleted by the stack
re: @alwa-nordic 's comment: you could add a "bt/mes/somekey" setting for that.
